passage:
"Mummy, you called Dr Iyer's office again?" Mahima asked.
"Only to ask about the reports. Beta, just eat, I'll handle the forms."
"Mummy, I love you, but I want the reports myself. Yesterday you hid the scan letter in the drawer."
Sharmila's hands stopped. "I didn't want you to be frightened."
"I'm more frightened when I don't know. Please come to the appointments, I'd like you there. But I'll decide about my treatment, and you can ask me anything."
"Anything?"
"The hard parts too. I can hold them."
Sharmila wiped her eyes on her dupatta. "I only know how to cook and worry."
"Then cook, and worry out loud. I'll answer."

qa.q: Where did Sharmila hide the scan letter?
qa.a: She hid the scan letter in the drawer.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila hide the scan letter?
qa.a: She did not want Mahima to be frightened. The hiding comes from fear and love, not from wanting to deceive.

qa.q: What did Mahima ask for regarding the appointments and the decisions?
qa.a: Mahima asked Sharmila to come to the appointments, said the treatment decisions would be Mahima's own, and invited questions about even the hard parts.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sharmila to say "I only know how to cook and worry"?
qa.a: She probably feels helpless and scared. Being invited to worry out loud gives her a role that Mahima can accept. 🤍

grounding: Parents hover and hide news out of fear that is love; Mahima says what help is wanted, what Mahima decides alone, and that the hard parts can be shared.

passage: When I told my group chat about the diagnosis, four friends replied within minutes. Yash didn't, and then Yash didn't for three weeks. I checked my phone more than I want to admit. It hurt, like being crossed off a list. But I remembered how stiff and awkward Yash had been at a cousin's funeral, and I wondered if this was the same. So I sent a plain message: "I'm not after wise words. A text about nothing, or a chai visit, would mean a lot." An hour later Yash replied with a bad joke about hospital food, and on Saturday turned up with samosas, standing in the doorway until I laughed. I keep the four who stayed close too. — Rashmi

qa.q: How long did Yash stay silent?
qa.a: Yash stayed silent for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel crossed off a list, and what made Rashmi doubt that reading?
qa.a: The silence hurt. Then Rashmi recalled Yash being stiff and awkward at a cousin's funeral, which hinted at discomfort rather than lack of care.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Rashmi told Yash plainly what would help, a text or a chai visit. That took away the worry about finding the right words.

qa.q: What might Yash have been feeling during the three weeks of silence?
qa.a: Probably discomfort and not knowing what to say. The joke about hospital food and the samosas suggest Yash did care.

grounding: A friend disappears after a diagnosis, likely from discomfort not lack of care; the person says how to help and keeps those who stay close.

passage:
Farida: hey. I heard. I don't know what to say so I'll just say I'm here
Nandini: thanks. I didn't want to tell anyone yet
Farida: no pressure to reply fast. I won't ask for details unless you want to share them
Nandini: honestly I'm just scared
Farida: that makes sense. I'm not going to tell you it'll all be fine. I'd rather listen
Nandini: ok. that actually helps
Farida: can I bring dinner Thursday? I'll leave it at the door if you want quiet
Farida: I'm also free to drive you to the hospital next week. Just tell me the day
Nandini: Thursday dinner would be really good. and the ride, maybe Tuesday
Farida: Tuesday it is. I'll be there at nine

qa.q: What did Farida offer to bring on Thursday?
qa.a: Farida offered to bring dinner.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when replying "honestly I'm just scared"?
qa.a: Nandini was afraid, and the reply shows some trust, since Nandini had not wanted to tell anyone yet.

qa.q: Which of Farida's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Farida listened instead of offering comfort like "it'll all be fine," and offered specific help, dinner and a ride, so Nandini need not think up a request.

qa.q: What might Farida have been afraid of before writing the first message?
qa.a: Saying the wrong thing. The opening line, "I don't know what to say," admits that worry openly.

grounding: A friend is ill and Farida fears the wrong words; Farida shows up, listens more than fixes, avoids clichés and offers specific help.

passage:
"Zainab, my neighbour swears there's a healer who cures it in a week," Aditi said. "He says stop the hospital medicine."
Zainab shook her head. "No. I've been up at dawn every day for my prayers, and honestly it holds me together. When I'm on that mat, the fear goes quiet."
"So you'd rather stay with the hospital?"
"I'd stay with both. I pray, and I go to my Thursday treatment. Nobody gets to swap one for the other."
"What would you like from me?"
"Sit with me on Thursday. And if my aunts bring a blessed thread, I'll wear it. I'll just also take my medicine."
Aditi laughed softly. "Deal."

qa.q: What did the neighbour's healer say Zainab should stop?
qa.a: The healer said to stop the hospital medicine.

qa.q: Why does Zainab say prayer "holds me together"?
qa.a: On the prayer mat her fear goes quiet, so prayer gives her steadiness and comfort.

qa.q: How can Zainab combine faith and treatment?
qa.a: Keep the dawn prayers and accept blessings from family, while continuing the Thursday treatment and her medicine.

qa.q: How might Aditi see the healer's promise of a cure in a week?
qa.a: Aditi probably worries that it could replace real treatment, which is why Aditi raised it and then asked how to help.

grounding: Prayer and ritual bring solace in illness; Zainab lets faith hold her and also follows treatment, refusing a miracle promise that replaces medicine.

passage: In the lane of small shops in the kasba, Kamal used to run up the stairs to his shop two at a time. Now he took them one by one, counting, and joked to his sister Rukmini, "See, my knees have joined a slow union." She laughed, and then the smile faded. The illness had taken his long days. Instead of pretending, he shortened the shop hours, put a stool behind the counter, and asked his nephew to carry the heavy sacks. "I used to want the biggest shop in town," he told her over tea. "Now I want to still be the man who knows every customer's name." He kept his ledger neat and his jokes sharp. Rukmini refilled his cup.

qa.q: How did Kamal now take the stairs to his shop?
qa.a: He took them one by one, counting.

qa.q: What does "I want to still be the man who knows every customer's name" suggest Kamal now cares about?
qa.a: He has redefined his goals, valuing dignity and connection with customers over having the biggest shop.

qa.q: What did Kamal do to live within his limits, and what else could he try?
qa.a: He shortened the shop hours, added a stool and asked his nephew to carry the sacks. He could keep asking for help wherever limits show up.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel about Kamal's jokes?
qa.a: She laughed, but her smile faded, so she likely enjoys his humour while also feeling what the illness has cost him. 🤍

grounding: Learning to live with limits and finding what still matters: acceptance as choosing how to spend energy, asking for help, redefining goals, keeping humour.

passage:
"You didn't even take your shoes off," Irawati said. "Sarika, what happened?"
"Same as always. Dilip sir sent another 'quick' task at seven. Thirty of those this week. Nobody says thanks, they just send the next one."
"You've been like this every Sunday night."
"I know. I dread Monday like a dentist appointment. I don't even care about the project any more." Sarika kicked her bag. "I feel bitter, and that's not who I am."
"So what will you do? Not just carry it and be a martyr."
"Talk to him. Show him the list. Ask what can wait." Sarika breathed out. "And take the leave days I've been hoarding."
"I'll pack snacks for the trip."

qa.q: How many quick tasks did Sarika say had arrived that week?
qa.a: Sarika said thirty of them had arrived that week.

qa.q: What does Sarika's dread of Monday, like a dentist appointment, reveal?
qa.a: It shows exhaustion and bitterness. Sarika no longer cares about the project and feels this is not the person Sarika wants to be.

qa.q: What plan did Sarika settle on?
qa.a: To talk to Dilip sir with the list of tasks, ask what can wait, and take the leave days.

qa.q: How does Irawati see Sarika carrying it all quietly?
qa.a: Irawati worries it will turn into silent martyrdom, so asks what Sarika will actually do about it.

grounding: Endless deadlines without thanks breed bitterness and Sunday dread; mature action is talking to the manager about load and taking leave.

passage: The day I fell asleep mid-sentence in a client call, my first thought wasn't "I'm exhausted." It was "I'm being lazy." I'm Hansa, Arohi, and that's the honest bit you asked me to tell. For months I'd worked through headaches and skipped meals, telling myself resting was for people with less to do. My friends stopped inviting me because I always said no. Then one Sunday I couldn't get out of bed, and I cried, not from sadness but from being empty. My sister made me see a doctor. I slept, I walked in the evenings, I ate proper meals and I met friends without my laptop. It felt like cheating at first. Now I know I was overloaded, not weak.

qa.q: What happened to Hansa during the client call?
qa.a: Hansa fell asleep mid-sentence.

qa.q: Why did Hansa think "I'm being lazy" rather than "I'm exhausted"?
qa.a: Hansa believed resting was for people with less to do, so tiredness felt like guilt instead of a warning.

qa.q: What could Hansa do to avoid sliding back into overwork?
qa.a: Keep sleeping, walking, eating proper meals and seeing friends, and go back to the doctor if the exhaustion returns.

qa.q: How might Hansa's friends have seen the constant refusals?
qa.a: As being turned away again and again, which may be why they stopped inviting. It does not mean they stopped caring.

grounding: Rest feels lazy while the body pleads; burnout signals overload not weakness, with sleep, movement, food, friends and professional help.

passage: Counsellor's note, Nirmala. Tenzin came to see me after the third weekend of working. The boss praises Tenzin's dedication in every meeting, "our most reliable person," and each time hands over another project. Tenzin laughed while describing this, but the laugh was thin, and Tenzin's eyes were red. I can't tell how much is tiredness and how much is worry about saying no. Together we made a two-week log of tasks and hours. Then Tenzin drafted a short list of priorities, with the items that could wait, to take to the boss on Monday, plus one plain sentence: "I can do A or B this week, which matters more?" We agreed that health comes before praise. I'll see Tenzin again next Friday.

qa.q: What did Tenzin and Nirmala make together?
qa.a: They made a two-week log of tasks and hours.

qa.q: What might Tenzin be feeling, given the thin laugh and red eyes?
qa.a: Probably tiredness and worry about saying no, though Nirmala admits the balance is unclear.

qa.q: What could Tenzin say when the boss hands over another task?
qa.a: "I can do A or B this week, which matters more?", along with the list of priorities and the log of hours.

qa.q: How might the boss see Tenzin's heavy workload?
qa.a: Possibly as a reward for reliability, and the boss may not notice the load it creates.

grounding: A boss praises dedication and piles on more; documenting workload, proposing priorities and being ready to say no.

passage: Three months of eleven o'clock dinners, that's what it was. I'm Sachin, and my partner Chandrika had gone quiet and snappy, jumping at every little thing I said. First I thought I'd done something wrong. Then I saw the laptop glow at midnight and understood: it wasn't me, it was the overwork. So one evening I said, gently, "I miss you. I'm not angry, I just miss you." We started a small ritual, tea on the balcony every Friday, phones inside. I also stopped pretending everything was fine, because quietly putting up with it wasn't helping either of us. Chandrika booked two days off. It didn't fix everything, but the snapping eased, and we laughed properly last week.

qa.q: What ritual did Sachin and Chandrika start?
qa.a: They started tea on the balcony every Friday, with phones inside.

qa.q: What did Sachin first think about Chandrika's quiet, snappy mood, and what changed that view?
qa.a: At first Sachin thought something was wrong with Sachin's own behaviour. Seeing the laptop glow at midnight showed it was the overwork.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say "I miss you" rather than complaining?
qa.a: It names the feeling without blame and invites closeness, and it did not treat the exhaustion as rejection.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt on hearing "I'm not angry, I just miss you"?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved and cared for rather than accused. Booking two days off suggests the message got through.

grounding: A partner withdrawn and irritable from overwork: Sachin says gently 'I miss you', proposes a small ritual and does not take it as rejection or enable it silently.

passage: Sunday, 11 pm. Uma didn't say a word when I got home at ten again, just kept the book open on the same page. Then: "I had dinner alone four times this week." I started to defend myself, the launch, the deadline, and stopped. I could hear how it sounded. It's true, and I hadn't noticed the days piling up until Uma counted them. I'm not proud. I don't want resentment to set in before I fix it. So tonight I said my laptop closes at seven on weekdays, no exceptions unless it's a real emergency, and we're taking Saturday to go to the lake, phones off. Uma smiled a little. The work matters, but what's it worth if the flat feels empty when I'm in it? — Pankaj

qa.q: At what time will Pankaj's laptop close on weekdays?
qa.a: It will close at seven.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj stop in the middle of defending?
qa.a: Pankaj heard how the excuses sounded and admitted that what Uma said was true, with the days piling up unnoticed.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to make the shut-off time hold?
qa.a: Keep it consistently, tell the team about it, be fully present at home and keep the Saturday plan for the lake.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt through the week of lone dinners?
qa.a: Alone and quiet, judging by the unturned page and the count of dinners. The small smile suggests some hope.

grounding: Work swallows the evenings and the partner feels alone; noticing it early, setting a shut-off time, planning a shared day and being present.
